Overview

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) updates its January 2025 analysis of generative-AI misuse and reports a shift: attackers now deploy malware that uses AI during execution, not only AI for productivity. Table 1 lists five families seen in 2025. PROMPTFLUX, an experimental VBScript dropper found in early June 2025, sends a hard-coded API key and a prompt to Gemini asking for antivirus-evading VBScript; one variant asks Gemini to rewrite the whole script every hour. PROMPTSTEAL, used by APT28 against Ukraine and reported by CERT-UA as LAMEHUG, queries Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct through the Hugging Face API for one-line Windows commands, which it runs blindly before sending the results out; GTIG calls it the first malware it has seen querying an LLM in live operations. PROMPTLOCK is a proof-of-concept ransomware that has an LLM write Lua scripts. QUIETVAULT steals GitHub and npm tokens and has AI command-line tools installed on the host search for other secrets. FRUITSHELL, a PowerShell reverse shell, carries prompts meant to defeat LLM-based security analysis. The rest of the report covers actors who tried to talk Gemini past its safeguards by posing as capture-the-flag players, students or researchers (a China-nexus actor got useful exploitation help this way), and state actors from China, Iran and North Korea who used Gemini at every stage of an intrusion: reconnaissance, phishing lures, exploit research, C2 development, data exfiltration and, in one case, an attempt to build an agent that turns questions into SQL over personal data. The report also covers an underground market for AI tools that almost always advertise phishing support, and North Korean deepfake lures. Most cases end with Google's response: disabled accounts and assets, and stronger classifiers and model.

Limits

  • Two of the five families are experimental. PROMPTFLUX's self-modification function is commented out and GTIG says it cannot compromise a victim network or device; PROMPTLOCK is a proof of concept.
  • Few numbers. No counts of victims, samples or prompts; the findings rest on Google's visibility, chiefly of Gemini use.
  • Assessments, not proof. Attribution is GTIG's, and some claims are hedged: PROMPTSTEAL "likely" uses stolen API tokens, and PROMPTFLUX is unattributed, linked to financially motivated actors only through its lure file names.
  • Unmeasured mitigations. Google says it strengthened its classifiers and the model, but gives no measurement.
  • Two forms of one text. The blog post states that it includes the report in full. The PDF digested here also carries the text of the attack-lifecycle figures; the blog post shows PROMPTSTEAL's two prompts as text (Figures 2 and 3), where the PDF shows them as images.
